title: Groupe de Galois motivique : notes manuscrites (s.d.), lettre (1965).

deep.reconstruction:
Context (pp.16-18). In this 1965 letter Grothendieck proposes that 'modular varieties' 𝔛/Γ should carry algebraic structures over Q, and usually over Z. Here 𝔛 is the G(R)-conjugacy class of a homomorphism i_0 : U_R → G_R from the circle group, for a reductive Q-group G, and Γ ⊂ G(Q) is commensurable with G(Z). Such 𝔛/Γ should carry a 'modular family' of Hodge structures and be moduli spaces of motives with extra structure. On this page he singles out the basic special case.

The data:
- V is a finite-dimensional Q-vector space with a nondegenerate form φ, either symmetric or alternating.
- G = SO(φ), the special isometry group; in the alternating case this is Sp(φ).
- i_0 : U_R → G_R satisfies i_0(-1) = id if φ is symmetric (even weight) and i_0(-1) = -id if φ is alternating (odd weight).
- i_0 defines a bigrading V_C = ⊕V^{pq} with V^{qp} equal to the conjugate of V^{pq}.
- A positivity condition holds, which he does not write down. In modern terms these are the Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations: φ(x, C ȳ) is definite, with C = i_0(i) the Weil operator.

The resulting orbit 𝔛 is 'a direct generalization of Siegel's half-plane'. It classifies all Hodge structures on V polarized by φ with prescribed Hodge numbers dim V^{pq}. In modern language 𝔛 is the classical (Griffiths) period domain D = G(R)/V, an open G(R)-orbit in a flag variety.

The 'trouble' is that these special 𝔛/Γ are universal, completed on p.18. Any (G, i_0), after a faithful polarized representation, maps into such a period domain, so every modular family is induced from one on a classical period domain. Hence if the tautological family on the classical 𝔛/Γ were motivic, every modular family would be. Now take G(R) compact. Then 𝔛 = 𝔛/Γ is a compact simply connected flag variety G_C/P (Borel). This would give a nonconstant polarized family of motives over a simply connected projective variety, contradicting Tate's conjectures, i.e. a rigidity argument. So Grothendieck concludes he does not know what to believe.

Modern resolution, absent from the page:
- The tautological family on a general period domain is not a variation of Hodge structure because it violates Griffiths transversality.
- Only horizontal families come from geometry.
- Algebraicity of 𝔛/Γ holds exactly in the Hermitian symmetric case, Deligne's Shimura-datum axiom that Ad∘h has types (-1,1),(0,0),(1,-1).
- Griffiths-Robles-Toledo (2014) proved that quotients of non-classical period/flag domains are not algebraic.

The page thus sits at the exact point where the 'all Mumford-Tate domains are moduli of motives' hope breaks down.
errors: Notation: for alternating φ the group should be Sp(φ); 'SO(φ)' is acceptable only as 'isometries of determinant 1', which for alternating forms is all of Sp.

The positivity condition is omitted. Without it the symmetric case would include non-polarized bigradings, and the orbit statement (G(R)-transitivity on polarized HS with fixed Hodge numbers) needs it; with it, the signature of φ is forced by the Hodge numbers.

Implicit gap (made explicit on p.18): the claim that the tautological family on 𝔛 is a 'Hodge family' ignores Griffiths transversality. That is the actual source of the 'trouble', which Grothendieck attributes instead to a possible conflict with Tate's conjecture.

ideas.what: Describing a Hodge structure on V as a homomorphism i_0 from the circle group U_R into G_R, with weight parity read from i_0(-1) = ±id
ideas.modern_name: Hodge structure as h: U(1) (or Deligne torus S) → G_R; Mumford-Tate/Deligne formalism
ideas.usually_credited_to: Mumford (Families of abelian varieties, Boulder 1965/1966); Deligne (Travaux de Shimura 1971, Hodge II)

ideas.what: The space of φ-polarized Hodge structures on V with fixed Hodge numbers as a G(R)-orbit generalizing the Siegel upper half-space
ideas.usually_credited_to: P. Griffiths (Periods of integrals on algebraic manifolds I-II, 1968)

ideas.what: Universality: every Mumford-Tate domain embeds equivariantly in a classical period domain via a faithful polarized representation, so modular families are induced from classical ones
ideas.modern_name: Mumford-Tate domains as subdomains of period domains

ideas.what: Expectation that 𝔛/Γ are algebraic over Q (and Z) and are moduli of motives, plus a self-refutation via compact G(R) (flag varieties) and Tate's conjecture
ideas.modern_name: Shimura varieties as moduli of motives; non-algebraicity of non-classical period domain quotients; Griffiths transversality

missed.claim: In 1965, before Griffiths' 1968 papers, Grothendieck independently defined classical period domains of polarized Hodge structures as a group-theoretic generalization of Siegel's half-space, with Hodge structures encoded as homomorphisms from the circle group.
missed.quote: Then [𝔛] is a direct generalization of Siegel's half-plane, and classifies all Hodge-structures with underlying Q-vector space V ... compatible with φ (i.e. φ is a polarization)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical priority and context: it shows the Mumford-Tate/period-domain picture was in Grothendieck's motivic program by 1965, contemporaneous with Mumford's Boulder paper.

missed.claim: Grothendieck detects (pp.17-18) that the 'all 𝔛/Γ are moduli of motives' expectation leads to a contradiction, but does not find the resolution (Griffiths transversality / Hermitian-symmetric condition). The thread was resolved later by others.
missed.quote: The trouble is that, as these special types of 𝔛, 𝔛/Γ are in a way "universal" for all others
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This documents an early recognition of the obstruction behind Griffiths-Robles-Toledo's non-algebraicity theorem and Deligne's Shimura axioms. It is of historical rather than new mathematical value.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is now standard (period domains, Mumford-Tate domains, the need for transversality). But a 1965 Grothendieck formulation predating Griffiths' published period domains, using the h-formalism, together with his self-diagnosed contradiction, is a notable and little-known historical detail.
transcription_corrections: 'Then [?] is a direct generalization' should read 'Then 𝔛 is a direct generalization' (the domain 𝔛 of p.16).
'with an fundamental bilinear form' should read 'with a fundamental bilinear form'.

The inserted marginal text reads approximately 'and a positivity condition of φ relative to the bigrading of V_C defined by i_0, which I will not write down', replacing a struck-out 'i(i) ... trivial'.
'𝔛, 𝔛/Γ' at the bottom: the handwriting shows script 𝔛 (written like 'V' in the neighbouring transcriptions), i.e. the same domain symbol.
